title: How I smoke-tested two browser renderers for BOTF Remastered 0.1.568
author: biggdogg420
selftext:
I’ve been remaking Birth of the Federation in Godot. It’s a turn-based Star Trek 4X where you scout systems, develop colonies and manage an empire. Claude Code has helped with implementation on the 3D title menu and tactical camera and flight controls. I direct the project and iterate on the builds rather than treating a successful export as the finish line.

For the 0.1.568 browser beta I used the same short check in WebGL and WebGPU: fresh Federation campaign, turn-zero galaxy map, select Sol, open its colony screen. Both made it through. Keeping the route fixed gives me a way to separate a first-load/renderer problem from a shared gameplay problem. It doesn’t tell me whether old saves work or whether a late-game turn stays fast.

The desktop browser build is free to try: https://botf-remastered.thabiggdogg420.chatgpt.site/play/

For those shipping AI-assisted games to the web: what would you automate next when moving from a smoke test to a gameplay regression test? I’m particularly interested in how you check that a save restores the same state, not just that the load screen goes away.

replies.author: biggdogg420
replies.body: Thanks, the public links are exactly what I was looking for. Starting with combat is an interesting choice. What was hardest to get to feel like BOTF: how orders resolve together, or how the ships move once the round starts?

replies.author: count023
replies.body:
I went with combat precisely because it was the hardest and everyone else went about the strategic maps and such more than the combat, so i wanted to get the hardest thing finished first. 

I'd say the balance and the AI interaction was the hardest to do, because i'd done feature enhancements out of the box like removing the unnecessary physics engine for the projectiles to display, and adding tilting, banking, avoidance cones, stuff like that. the actual implementation of stuff like camera work and the weapons fire itself was pretty rudamentary. the entire combat engine inside BOTF was basically Falcon 4 which was an air dogfighting game, so most what seemed like it's hard to do was just really cumbersome. 

the big bit i'm happy with is the moddability and expandability, if you look under the hood you'll see how scalable the game is, everything is a type-object deployment, adding ships, special efects, weapons, all tunable as data, so the game can have as many or as few combinations as you can mod into it with relative ease, no hard coded back end or anything of that sort. I took inspiration from armada and stellaris to pull it off.

replies.author: biggdogg420
replies.body: That makes sense. Data-driven ships and weapons make it easier to add a hull, but every new combination gives the AI another choice to get wrong. Was there a particular matchup you kept replaying to tell whether a balance or AI change had actually helped?
